When Your Furnace Stops Heating

A sudden drop in indoor temperature is usually the first sign something is wrong. You might hear the thermostat click, but the furnace never fires up, or perhaps the blower runs endlessly, pushing only lukewarm air through your vents. During one of our sudden Texas Northers, losing heat goes from a minor inconvenience to a serious problem within hours. Many heating failures actually stem from the system sitting dormant during our long, hot summers. Dust accumulates, electrical connections can oxidize, and when that first true cold front hits Elgin, the furnace struggles to ignite or sustain a flame. If your system is blowing cold air, short-cycling, or making unusual noises, immediate attention is required. If you need urgent assistance after hours, we offer emergency heating repair.

Common Furnace Problems We Diagnose

Ignition Failures

Modern gas furnaces rely on hot surface ignitors rather than standing pilot lights. Over time, the silicon carbide material in these ignitors degrades and cracks, preventing the furnace from lighting the burners.

Flame Sensor Issues

If your furnace lights for a few seconds and then shuts down, the flame sensor is likely dirty or failing. A microscopic layer of oxidation can stop the sensor from detecting the burner flame, prompting the control board to shut the gas valve as a safety precaution.

Blower Motor and Capacitor Problems

The blower motor pushes heated air through your ductwork. If the start capacitor weakens, the motor may hum but fail to spin. Continued strain can cause the motor itself to burn out, leading to zero airflow.

Heat Exchanger Concerns

The heat exchanger separates the combustion gases from the air circulating in your home. Years of thermal expansion and contraction can cause metal fatigue, leading to cracks. This is a critical safety issue that demands immediate attention.

Gas Valve Failures

The gas valve controls fuel flow to the burners. If the solenoid fails or the valve sticks, you will experience either no heat or a dangerously erratic flame.

Thermostat and Control Board Malfunctions

Sometimes the furnace is fine, but the thermostat is miscalibrated or the integrated furnace control (IFC) board has a burnt relay, preventing it from sending the correct signals to start the heating cycle.

Gas Furnaces vs. Electric Furnaces vs. Heat Pumps

Homes in the 78621 area utilize a mix of heating technologies, and each requires a different diagnostic approach. Gas furnaces provide powerful, fast heat but require strict safety checks of the combustion process, draft inducer, and gas pressure. Electric furnaces (often part of an air handler) use heavy-duty heating elements and sequencers; repairs here focus heavily on high-voltage electrical testing and checking for burnt wire connections. Heat pumps, very common in Central Texas, operate differently by transferring heat from outside to inside. When a heat pump fails in winter, the issue might be a frozen outdoor coil, a faulty reversing valve, or a malfunctioning defrost control board rather than a traditional furnace problem.

What Happens During a Furnace Diagnostic Visit

When you call (877) 361-0428, we follow a systematic diagnostic process to pinpoint the exact point of failure. We don't guess; we test. First, we verify the thermostat call for heat. Then, we check the control board for error fault codes. We will measure the electrical draw of the draft inducer motor and verify that the pressure switch closes properly. Next, we test the resistance of the hot surface ignitor and measure the microamps generated by the flame sensor. Finally, we inspect the blower motor's amp draw and check the high-limit switch to ensure the system isn't overheating. Once we identify the failing component, we explain the issue clearly and provide a firm price for the repair.

Furnace Repair vs. Replacement: Making the Right Decision

We aim to repair whenever it is practical and cost-effective. However, as heating equipment ages past 12-15 years, the frequency and cost of repairs can escalate. If you are facing a massive repair bill—such as replacing a cracked heat exchanger or a failed proprietary control board—on an older out-of-warranty system, putting that money toward a new furnace installation might be the smarter financial choice. We will give you an honest assessment of your equipment's overall condition, factoring in its age, efficiency, and safety, so you can decide what makes the most sense for your home and budget.

Safety Concerns: Carbon Monoxide, Gas Leaks, and Electrical Hazards

Safety is the primary reason why DIY furnace repair is heavily discouraged. Gas furnaces rely on a precisely balanced combustion process. A cracked heat exchanger, a blocked flue pipe, or a misadjusted gas valve can result in carbon monoxide spilling into your living space—an odorless, colorless gas that is incredibly dangerous. Additionally, older gas connections can develop slow leaks. On the electrical side, modern furnaces utilize high-voltage components and sensitive low-voltage control circuits; a simple mistake can result in electrical shocks or permanently fry an expensive control board. Our technicians are trained to identify and mitigate these hazards during every service call.

What You Can Check Before Calling for Repair

Before scheduling a service call, you can perform a few basic checks. First, check your air filter. A severely clogged filter restricts airflow, which can cause the furnace to overheat and trip the high-limit switch, shutting the system down. Replace it if it's dirty. Second, verify your thermostat is set to 'Heat' and the temperature is set higher than the current room temperature. Check the batteries if it has a blank screen. Finally, check your electrical panel to ensure the breaker for the furnace (or air handler) hasn't tripped. If these basic steps don't resolve the issue, it's time to call in a professional.

Why Central Texas Winter Weather Demands Reliable Heating

While Bastrop County is known for intense summer heat, our winters are unpredictable. We can experience weeks of mild weather followed by a sudden plunge into freezing temperatures. Because our homes are built primarily for cooling, they can lose heat rapidly during a hard freeze. This makes a reliable furnace essential for protecting your plumbing from freezing and keeping your family safe. Regular heating maintenance in the fall can help prepare your system for these sudden workload spikes, but when unexpected breakdowns occur during a freeze warning, you need a local repair team that can respond quickly and fix the problem right the first time.

5

6

Check the blower motor capacitor and measure operating voltage/amperage.
